rationale: Asks for the most likely effect of the Navigation Acts on Atlantic port cities — explaining the effect of a mercantilist policy (Causation); content is transatlantic trade.

Asks how plantation demand for enslaved labor connects to the Middle Passage leg of the triangular trade — explaining the relationship between two developments; content is the transatlantic slave trade.
Asks which argument about mercantilism and the colonies is best supported by the period's evidence — making a historically defensible claim; content is mercantilist trade policy.

Asks what the Bell 1876 telephone patent drawing, as a document, shows — identifying the source's purpose (a legal claim of ownership) and what it can support; content is Gilded Age technological innovation.
Asks for the incandescent bulb's most important economic effect — explaining the effect of a technological development (extended usable business hours); content is electrification.

Asks what the Menlo Park laboratory photograph shows about the organization of invention — identifying the claim the non-text source supports (invention as organized, business-funded team work); content is industrial research.
Asks which feature of electrification the Pearl Street line-laying engraving illustrates — explaining the development (an entirely new infrastructure); content is electrification.

Asks for Pearl Street's most important innovation — identifying the connection between the technology (central station) and the new business model (power as a utility service); content is electrification.
Asks the name of the steelmaker's strategy of owning every production stage — identifying the concept vertical integration; content is industrial consolidation.
Asks why the Bessemer process mattered most — explaining the effect of a technological development (cheap steel for rails, bridges, buildings); content is steel technology.

Asks which technology-business relationship the Eads Bridge illustrates — identifying the feedback loop (cheaper steel enabled giant projects, which then created more steel demand); content is steel and business.
Asks what made the Brooklyn Bridge possible only at that time — identifying the broader context (cheap steel after the Bessemer process) for the development; content is steel technology.

Asks the cartoonist's main point in the Vanderbilt 'Modern Colossus' cartoon — identifying the source's point of view (railroad corporations dominating the economy, threatening democratic control); content is railroad corporate power.
Asks what railroad expansion most directly made possible — explaining the effect of the development (a continental national market); content is railroads and industrial capitalism.

Asks what the 'Bosses of the Senate' cartoon best supports as evidence; the explanation warns against overreading (a cartoon shows perceived influence, not provable bribery) — explaining the source's significance and limits; content is corporate influence on the federal government.
Asks the name of Rockefeller's strategy of buying rival refineries — identifying the concept horizontal integration; content is Standard Oil.

Asks which statement about trusts is best supported by the historical record — judging how evidence supports claims (trusts killed competition; the Sherman Act was weakly enforced); content is trusts.

Asks what weak enforcement of the Sherman Act illustrates — situating the development within the broader context of the era's pro-business federal stance; content is antitrust and the government's role.

Asks what the Edison-versus-Carnegie/Rockefeller contrast illustrates — identifying the pattern that organizing capital and markets captured more wealth than inventing alone; content is Gilded Age capitalism.
Asks the telephone's most important effect on businesses — explaining the effect (instant coordination making national-scale companies practical); content is communications technology.
Asks how the typewriter changed business — explaining the effect (paperwork and communication at corporate scale); content is office technology.
Asks what the ICC is best understood as — situating the first federal railroad regulation within the broader context of farmers' anger over uncontrollable rates; content is railroad regulation.
Asks which pairing matches each side's evidence in the debate over who benefited from the Gilded Age economy — comparing the defenders' and critics' arguments; content is the Gilded Age economy.

Asks the best historical criticism of the claim that the bulb 'single-handedly created the modern American city' — explaining how evidence refutes an overreaching claim (systems required; cities already growing); content is the electric system.
Asks which strategy Rockefeller's Standard Oil used to dominate refining — identifying the concept (horizontal integration via buying rival refineries); content is Standard Oil.
Asks why large corporations employed growing white-collar workforces — explaining the cause of the development (paperwork, accounts, coordination across operations); content is the new middle class.

Asks how the typewriter changed the office workforce's makeup — explaining the effect (new clerical jobs of typist/stenographer largely filled by women); content is women entering the middle-class workforce.
Asks how department stores changed American shopping — explaining the development (fixed prices, advertised goods, brand names, shopping as leisure); content is consumer culture.

Asks which conclusion the 1902 Macy's floor plan best supports as evidence — judging what the source can establish (scale and deliberate organization) versus overreads about national habits or sales rankings; content is department stores.
Asks to whom mail-order catalogs mattered most — explaining the effect (customers in small towns and rural areas far from city stores); content is consumer culture.

Asks why electric streetcars created streetcar suburbs — explaining the mechanism (commuting from cheaper land farther out, separating home from work); content is suburbanization and the middle class.

Asks why schooling and leisure help explain the middle class's reform role — identifying the historical context for the development (the audience for clubs, temperance unions, muckrakers); content is the middle class and reform.

Asks what 'Progressivism's foot soldiers' points to — explaining how the Gilded Age middle class industrialization created relates to the Progressive Era's reform constituency; content is the middle class's reform role.

Asks whether the quoted claim about the middle class (industrialization's durable political product) is a reasonable judgment — making a historically defensible claim; content is the middle class and industrialization.
Asks how the white-collar middle class differed from factory workers — identifying the concept (salaried non-manual work, still subject to economic ups and downs); content is the middle class.

Asks which evidence would strongest support the claim that department stores made shopping leisure — identifying the supporting evidence (advertising, attractive display, browsing as pastime); content is consumer culture.
Asks what the Marshall Field warehouse photo's large scale best illustrates — identifying what the visual source shows (retail organized on an industrial scale); content is retail growth.
Asks why fixed advertised prices mattered — explaining the effect (predictable, impersonal transactions suited to a mass market of strangers); content is department-store retail.

Asks what pattern the middle class's buy-then-reform behavior illustrates — identifying continuity and change (kept faith in the economy's benefits while pushing to correct its harms); content is the middle class.
Asks how the typewriter and telephone contributed to women entering offices — explaining the cause (new clerical jobs of typist, stenographer, operator); content is women's workforce entry.

Asks what the department store represented compared with the general store — identifying the concept (retail organized on the same large scale as factories and railroads); content is consumer culture.
Asks what an 1890 department-store ad cannot by itself show — judging the limits of what the evidence supports (purchasing power, clerks' working conditions); content is department-store advertising.
Asks why streetcar suburbs made middle-class homeownership achievable — explaining the mechanism (affordable land farther out became practical to reach daily); content is suburbanization.

Asks what Grady's 1886 'New South' speech plus its setting (an Atlanta editor addressing New York businessmen) shows — identifying the source's purpose and audience (a pitch for reconciliation through commerce); content is the New South creed.
Asks how Grady says the New South will differ from the Old South — identifying the development (small farms and diversified industry replacing plantation slavery); content is the New South.

Asks the most serious limitation of Grady's speech as evidence of Southern farmers' actual conditions — explaining how the speaker's booster purpose and investor audience limit the source's use; content is the New South.

Asks what critics meant by calling the crop-lien system 'wage slavery in a new form' — identifying the claim in the critics' text (debt and legal control binding laborers to the land); content is sharecropping and tenant farming.

Asks how the 1895 Puck cartoon's 'triumph of free labor' claim holds against the historical evidence — judging that evidence modifies the source's claim (overstated: most Southerners stayed poor farmers); content is the New South.
Asks what a sharecropping contract shows landowners gained — identifying the concept (close control over tenants' labor and over when and how crops could be sold); content is sharecropping.

Asks which slavery-era feature the sharecropping contract most directly continued — identifying the continuing development (the landowner's control over the crop and the labor); content is sharecropping.

Asks what an 1867 sharecropping contract is most valuable for showing as a primary source — identifying the source's evidentiary value (its legal terms binding tenants to landowners); content is sharecropping.
Asks what the Birmingham bird's-eye view best illustrates — identifying the development (genuine but limited New South industrial growth); content is Southern industrialization.

Asks what conclusion the child-sweeper mill photo best supports about the New South's industrial promise — explaining the development's limits (low-wage labor, poverty persisted); content is Southern mills.
Asks what a single mill photograph cannot by itself establish — judging the limits of what the evidence supports (typicality across mills, wages); content is Southern child labor.

Asks the purpose of poll-tax requirements in the 1890s Southern constitutions — identifying the development (making registration costly and difficult to strip Black men of the vote); content is New South disfranchisement.

Asks why the 'understanding clause' worked as a disfranchisement tool — explaining how the constitutional text's evidence supports the claim (registrar discretion to pass whites and fail Blacks); content is disfranchisement.
Asks the effect of grandfather clauses — explaining the development (protected poor whites while poll taxes and literacy tests excluded Black voters); content is disfranchisement.

Asks which conclusion the evidence best supports about how much the New South broke from the Old — making a historically defensible claim (only partly new: real industry, but coercion echoed and the region stayed poorest); content is the New South.
Asks how recent immigration differed most clearly from 1960 by region of origin — describing the change (shift from Europe toward Latin America and Asia); content is post-1965 immigration.

Asks how 1990s/2000s nativism most resembled the Know-Nothings and 1920s restrictionism — identifying the recurring pattern (newcomers said to threaten jobs, culture, political stability); content is nativism.
Asks what 'majority-minority' means in the immigration-politics context — identifying the historical context term (no single racial or ethnic group a majority); content is demographic change.
Asks which decade the foreign-born share first crossed 10 percent — identifying the data point in the chart; content is post-1965 immigration.

Asks which statement best reflects economists' mainstream finding on immigration and wages — making a historically defensible claim (modest wage effects on less-skilled competing natives); content is immigration's wage effects.
Asks where immigrants found jobs and why — explaining how immigration relates to labor-market demand (jobs pulled migrants, migrants supplied labor); content is immigrant labor.

Asks what a historian comparing an 1850s nativist passage and a 1990s passage would conclude — explaining the shared point of view across the two sources (recycled claims about cultural and economic threat); content is nativist rhetoric.

Asks what the persistence of assimilation debates best shows — identifying the continuing development (each generation of newcomers revived the same argument about American identity); content is assimilation debates.
Asks which decade saw the largest increase in legal immigration over the prior decade — identifying the data in the chart; content is immigration levels.
Asks how the 1965 immigration act differed from the 1920s quota laws — identifying the historical context (national-origin preferences ended) for the development; content is the 1965 act.
Asks which mechanism explains the post-1965 climb — situating the development within the broader context of the act's family-reunification provisions (chain migration); content is the 1965 act.

Asks the key difference in long-term effects between the Bracero program and post-1965 immigration — explaining how temporary versus permanent admission relates to settlement and community impact; content is guest-worker versus family immigration.

Asks which push-pull combination best explains large Latin American immigration in the 1980s-2000s — explaining the causes (U.S. jobs and family ties as pull, poverty and instability as push); content is migration.
Asks what the chart's 1970 low point (4.7 percent) reflects — identifying what the data shows (decades of quota restrictions minimized immigration); content is restriction-era demographics.

Asks what a historian should consider about the grower's perspective — identifying the source's point of view (an employer with an economic interest in immigrant labor, which shapes but does not disqualify the testimony); content is immigration debate testimony.
Asks which earlier pattern the 2016 anti-immigration backlash most directly continued — identifying the recurring nativist politics that follows every large immigration wave; content is nativism.

Asks which evidence best evaluates the claim that America always had open immigration — supporting the counter-argument with specific evidence (the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act and 1920s quotas); content is immigration restriction history.

Asks which political debate intensified as the foreign-born share nearly tripled — explaining the effect of the demographic development (border enforcement, legalization, membership); content is immigration politics.
Asks which question the legal-immigration chart cannot answer — judging the source's boundaries (legal admissions only; silent on unauthorized immigration); content is immigration data.

Asks how post-1965 immigration resembled the Ellis Island era — identifying the historical context (labor demand and chain migration through family networks) for the development; content is post-1965 immigration.

Asks which earlier episode most closely resembles the 1965 act's policy reversal — identifying the analogous historical context (the 1943 repeal of the Chinese Exclusion Act); content is immigration policy reversal.

Asks which political development followed Latino population growth — identifying the connection (both parties competing for Latino voters, making immigration an electoral battleground); content is immigration and electoral politics.

Asks what Reagan's 'evil empire' language signaled versus the detente era — identifying the source's point of view (a return to moral confrontation with the USSR); content is Reagan's Cold War posture.
Asks which broader strategy SDI fit into — explaining the development (pressuring the USSR through an arms buildup its economy could not match); content is Reagan's Cold War strategy.

Asks which statement best supports the argument that Reagan's buildup caused the deficits — identifying the evidence supporting the argument (1981 tax cuts paired with the buildup, deficit tripled); content is Reagan-era deficits.
Asks what problems glasnost and perestroika were meant to fix — identifying the development (Soviet economic stagnation and one-party rigidity); content is Gorbachev's reforms.
Asks why the 1987 INF Treaty was historic — identifying the broader arms-control context (the first treaty ever to eliminate a whole class of nuclear weapons); content is the INF Treaty.

Asks for the correct sequence of the Cold War's European endgame — identifying the chronological development (the Wall falls 1989, Germany reunifies 1990, the USSR dissolves 1991); content is the Cold War's end.

Asks what a historian citing the buildup as a cause must also acknowledge — qualifying a single-cause argument with diverse evidence per the review's multi-causal rule (internal Soviet decay equally essential); content is Cold War causation.

Asks why the 1991 Gulf War exemplified Bush's 'new world order' — situating the development within the post-Cold War context (a broad UN-authorized coalition possible once the Soviet veto was gone); content is the Gulf War.

Asks how the Reagan Doctrine fit the broader strategy the spending chart shows — explaining the development (a cheaper complement to the buildup, backing anti-Soviet guerrillas); content is the Reagan Doctrine.

Asks how a historian should weigh Reagan's 'tear down this wall' speech against the INF Treaty — explaining the speech's purpose (public rhetoric pressuring Gorbachev) versus the treaty's serious negotiation; content is Reagan's Cold War diplomacy.

Asks how Reagan's approach differed from Nixon's detente — identifying the historical context (coexistence through negotiated limits versus buildup with confrontation, then negotiation); content is Reagan versus detente.

Asks what Iran-Contra most clearly revealed about the Reagan administration — identifying the connection (officials pursued anti-communist goals outside the law, deceiving Congress); content is Iran-Contra.

Asks why the 1980s oil-price collapse hurt the USSR especially badly — explaining the cause (the USSR lived on oil-export earnings just as the arms race demanded more spending); content is the Soviet economy.
Asks which Soviet decision made the 1989 Eastern European revolutions possible — explaining the cause (Gorbachev's refusal to use force, abandoning the Brezhnev Doctrine); content is 1989.

Asks which later development best challenges the 'end of history' claim — modifying the argument with diverse evidence (returned great-power rivalry, enduring authoritarianism, domestic polarization); content is post-Cold War triumphalism.

Asks what 1990 spending near Cold War peaks suggests about the expected 'peace dividend' — identifying the pattern (the dividend disappointed as new interventions added fresh demands); content is post-Cold War military spending.

Asks which internal development most directly caused the USSR itself to dissolve — judging how the evidence supports the nationalist-secession claim (republics declaring sovereignty hollowed the union); content is the Soviet collapse.

Asks what the unipolar moment meant for 1990s American foreign policy — situating the development within the broader context (fewer great-power constraints, interventions to uphold a liberal order); content is post-Cold War foreign policy.

Asks which post-Cold War American action shows the strongest continuity with containment — identifying the pattern (leading coalitions against aggression and atrocities, extending intervention to new causes); content is post-Cold War intervention.

Asks which interpretation of the Soviet collapse the 1991 news analysis passage is most useful for — identifying the source's argument/point of view (the internal-decay interpretation); content is Cold War historiography.

Compares how the American and Soviet systems handled the mid-1980s oil-price shock — explaining the systemic difference (flexible market economy absorbed it; the oil-dependent command economy could not); content is the Soviet economy.

Asks how the oil-price collapse compounded the cost of the Soviet war in Afghanistan — explaining the effect (falling oil revenues left Moscow less able to afford the stalemated war); content is Afghanistan and the Soviet fiscal crisis.

Asks the strongest rebuttal to the claim that SDI alone ended the Cold War — refuting a single-cause argument with evidence (SDI was never built; the broad buildup was only one cause among many); content is Cold War causation.
Asks why German reunification mattered beyond Germany — explaining the significance (it erased the Cold War's central dividing line in Europe); content is reunification.

Asks why NATO survived while the Warsaw Pact dissolved — explaining how the two alliances relate (a voluntary alliance kept by consent versus one imposed by Moscow); content is post-Cold War alliances.

Asks for which quality Bush's management of the Cold War's end is praised — situating his cautious stewardship within the broader context of a fragile nuclear transition; content is the Cold War's end.

Asks what consequence followed from the Cold War ending without a formal settlement — explaining how the evidence supports the claim (no postwar rules, NATO's role and Russia's place unsettled); content is the post-Cold War order.
Asks which element of the 1990s 'victory lap' the deficit-to-surplus chart documents — identifying the development (the fiscal turnaround amid the long expansion); content is the 1990s economy.
Asks the 9/11 attacks' most immediate historical significance — identifying the broader context (the open-ended War on Terror that reshaped foreign and domestic policy); content is 9/11.

Asks which statement best captures the Patriot Act debate — comparing the two sides' arguments (supporters citing necessity versus critics warning of eroded civil liberties); content is the Patriot Act.
Asks which sequence of events drove the 2000-2010 military-spending increase — explaining the causes (Afghanistan in 2001, then Iraq in 2003); content is the War on Terror.

Asks the chief political consequence of the Iraq War's false WMD justification — making a historically defensible evaluative claim (it discredited the neoconservative vision and split the country); content is the Iraq War.
Asks what the Bush doctrine of preemption held — identifying the doctrine within the broader context (a break from deterrence and containment); content is preemption.

Asks which comparison of 9/11's aftermath with earlier wartime power expansions is valid — identifying the recurring pattern (crisis expands federal power at liberty's expense, as with the Espionage Act, internment, McCarthyism); content is the Patriot Act.
Asks what the Department of Homeland Security's creation represented — identifying the development (the largest federal reorganization in decades, consolidating 22 agencies); content is DHS.

Asks which causes best explain the financial crisis following the housing bubble — explaining the causes (risky mortgages, deregulation-enabled leverage, financial engineering); content is the 2008 crisis.

Asks why the TARP bailouts angered the public — explaining how the rescues relate to the populist fury on left and right (taxpayers rescued reckless firms while homeowners got far less); content is the bailout backlash.

Compares the Great Recession with the Great Depression — explaining how the two crises relate (both began in financial collapse, but 2008's intervention was massive and fast); content is the two crises.

Asks what the review's later account suggests about the 'post-racial' reading of Obama's election — situating the event within the broader context of continued racial conflict (Black Lives Matter, demographic-change politics); content is Obama and race.
Asks why the ACA became the decade's defining political war — explaining the cause (the largest welfare-state expansion since the Great Society, seen as federal overreach); content is the ACA.
Asks what the Tea Party was primarily reacting against — identifying the connection (the bailouts, stimulus, and ACA seen as government overreach after the crisis); content is the Tea Party.
Asks what 'partisan sorting' means — identifying the concept (Americans clustering into like-minded communities so parties grew uniform internally and distant); content is polarization.

Asks why Bush v. Gore matters in the polarization story — explaining the significance (a 5-4 decision that effectively gave Bush the presidency and left the country evenly and bitterly divided); content is the 2000 election.
Asks how Clinton's impeachment fits the review's polarization account — identifying the connection (impeachment became a partisan weapon with party-line votes); content is the 1998 impeachment.

Asks why the Contract with America was significant — situating the 1994 GOP congressional takeover within its broader context (a nationalized small-government platform against the deficit backdrop); content is 1994.

Asks what the 1996 welfare reform law is best understood as — explaining the development (a Democratic president adopting conservative premises through Clinton's triangulation strategy); content is welfare reform.

Asks which statement best evaluates what drones changed and what they continued — making a historically defensible claim (kept the reliance on air power, but made remote targeted killing routine and contested); content is drone warfare.

Asks which groups' grievances Trump's 2016 coalition most directly expressed — situating the election within the broader context of the backlash against globalization, demographic change, and the establishment; content is 2016.
Asks which statement best describes the foreign-born share trend — identifying the claim the chart supports (nearly tripled, 4.7 to 13.7 percent, 1970-2020); content is post-1965 immigration.
Asks through which mechanism the 1965 law produced its decades-long 'long tail' — explaining the cause (family-reunification preferences created compounding chain migration); content is the 1965 act.

Asks what Clinton's triangulation shows about the era's political climate — situating the development within the broader context (limited-government ideas so dominant even a Democrat governed on their premises); content is 1990s politics.

Asks what Occupy and the Tea Party shared despite different ideologies — identifying the pattern (a shared conviction that elites had rigged the system against ordinary people); content is post-2008 populism.
Asks against which backdrop the COVID-19 pandemic unfolded — identifying the historical situation (institutional distrust and social-media fragmentation); content is COVID-19.
Asks how the review presents the January 6 attack — identifying the broader context (the violent peak of unresolved arguments about elections amid institutional distrust); content is January 6.

Asks which longer story Obergefell belongs to — identifying the continuing development (civil rights as an unfinished continuity from the 1960s through marriage equality and beyond); content is marriage equality.

Asks what Occupy, Black Lives Matter, and #MeToo share with the Tea Party — identifying the pattern (distrust of institutions, organizing outside traditional party machinery); content is 21st-century movements.
Asks how social-media fragmentation fuels polarization — explaining the mechanism (algorithmic feeds and self-selected networks hardening divisions); content is media fragmentation.

Asks which recent development best illustrates the domestic side of the review's through-line — supporting the argument with specific evidence (unresolved arguments about elections across three presidencies); content is the post-Cold War consensus.
Asks what Reagan's 1980 election repudiated — identifying the broader context (the New Deal/Great Society premise of activist federal government); content is the 1980 election.
Asks what supply-side theory claimed — identifying the concept (lower taxes would unleash enough growth to pay for the cuts); content is Reaganomics.
Asks what the deficit chart shows about supply-side theory's central prediction — explaining how the evidence refutes the claim (the prediction failed: tripled deficits); content is Reaganomics.
Asks what Reagan's firing of the PATCO strikers signaled — identifying the connection (organized labor's power was over; a confrontational stance employers copied); content is labor under Reagan.
Asks what Reagan's 'government is the problem' inaugural line signaled — identifying the source's point of view (a reversal of the liberal premise of federal power); content is Reagan's philosophy.

Asks which statement accurately contrasts Reagan's conservatism with the liberalism it displaced — identifying the two philosophies (federal power as threat to freedom and growth versus deliverer of security and justice); content is Reagan-era ideology.

Asks what supporters of deregulation argued — identifying the historical context (the deregulatory case: removing rate-setting and entry barriers to lower prices through competition); content is deregulation.

Asks which overall evaluation the review's Reaganomics verdict supports — making a historically defensible claim (a mixed verdict: renewed growth, failed fiscal promise, wider inequality); content is Reaganomics.

Asks which claim about the Reagan-Bush era the deficit chart best supports — identifying the evidence supporting the argument (tax cuts plus the military buildup produced sustained large deficits); content is Reagan-era deficits.
Asks why domestic spending cuts didn't prevent the deficits — explaining how the policies relate (savings could not cover the combined tax-cut-plus-buildup gap); content is Reagan-era deficits.
Asks what the 1981 Economic Recovery Tax Act did — identifying the development (cut individual income-tax rates substantially, the supply-side centerpiece); content is ERTA.

Asks what alternatives the 1980 election offered — identifying the broader context (Carter's active-government liberalism versus Reagan's shrink-at-home, rebuild-the-military conservatism); content is the 1980 election.
